objectives: Read a logarithm as the inverse of exponentiation.
Apply the product and power laws of logarithms.
Explain why log scales cover wide ranges in one picture.
Compute pH as a logarithm of concentration.

sections.body:
The logarithm of a number to a base is the exponent the base needs to reach it: log_b(x) = y means b^y = x. The common logarithm uses base 10, the natural logarithm uses base e, and both undo exponentiation.

**Logarithms turn multiplication into addition.** That single property made them the engine of calculation for three centuries, and it still drives the decibel, the Richter scale and the pH of a solution.

terms.gloss: The exponent to which a base must be raised to produce a number.
The number that is raised to a power; 10 in log10, e in ln.
The power to which a base is raised; the answer a logarithm gives.

sections.body: Two laws carry every computation. The log of a product is the sum of the logs, and the log of a power is the power times the log. Together they reduce any monster of multiplications to a short chain of additions.

equations.caption: The product law: multiplication becomes addition.
The power law: exponentiation becomes multiplication.

Add the terms and read the answer from the log table.

sections.body:
Some ranges are too wide for a ruler. The loudness of a whisper and of a jet engine differ by a factor of a trillion; on a linear scale one of them is invisible. A log scale draws each factor of ten as one equal step, and the whole range fits on one line.

Read the vertical axis of the plot as powers of ten: each grid line is ten times the one below it. The curve of y = 10^x becomes a straight climb.
examples: A solution with [H+] = 10^-7 mol/L has pH = −log10(10^-7) = 7: neutral water.

item.summary: A logarithm answers the question "how many times do I multiply?" It turns wide worlds — from the energy of an earthquake to the loudness of a concert — into numbers a person can hold.
